claim: Authentic peptide sequences were obtained from 3.8-Ma-old ostrich eggshell (OES) from the site of Laetoli, Tanzania.
source: Previously, we showed that authentic peptide sequences could be obtained from 3.8-Ma-old ostrich eggshell (OES) from the site of Laetoli, Tanzania (Demarchi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Demarchi et al., 2016

claim: The same peptide sequences survive in a >6.5 Ma OES recovered from a palaeosteppe setting in northwestern China.
source: Here, we show that the same sequences survive in a >6.5 Ma OES recovered from a palaeosteppe setting in northwestern China.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including LC-MS/MS analysis and peptide identification

claim: The eggshell is thicker than those observed in extant species.

claim: The eggshell is consistent with the Liushu Struthio sp. ootaxon.

claim: These findings push the preservation of ancient proteins back to the Miocene.
source: These findings push the preservation of ancient proteins back to the Miocene and highlight their potential for paleontology, paleoecology, and evolutionary biology.

claim: Ancient proteins have potential for paleontology, paleoecology, and evolutionary biology.
source: These findings push the preservation of ancient proteins back to the Miocene and highlight their potential for paleontology, paleoecology, and evolutionary biology.

claim: The oldest authenticated peptide sequences to date were reported in 2016 from 3.8-Ma-old ostrich eggshell from Laetoli, Tanzania.
source: The oldest authenticated peptide sequences to date were reported in 2016 from 3.8-Ma-old ostrich eggshell (OES) from the site of Laetoli, Tanzania (Demarchi et al., 2016).

claim: The 2016 Laetoli study integrated computational chemistry (molecular dynamics simulations) as well as experimental data to propose a mechanism of preservation.
source: This finding had great scientific impact since it integrated computational chemistry (molecular dynamics simulations) as well as experimental data to propose a mechanism of preservation, concluding that mineral binding ensures the survival of protein sequences.
evidence: Supported by citation to Demarchi et al., 2016

claim: Mineral binding ensures the survival of protein sequences.
source: This finding had great scientific impact since it integrated computational chemistry (molecular dynamics simulations) as well as experimental data to propose a mechanism of preservation, concluding that mineral binding ensures the survival of protein sequences.

claim: Peptide-bound amino acids can survive into deep time even in hot environments.
source: Importantly, this study demonstrated that peptide-bound amino acids could survive into deep time even in hot environments.

claim: Temperature affects the kinetics of protein diagenesis.
source: The effect of temperature on the kinetics of protein diagenesis has been described by several authors, both on the basis of actualistic experiments and of the quantification of the extent of degradation in ancient samples of known ages (Crisp et al., 2013; Demarchi et al., 2013; Hendy et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 1997; Kaufman, 2006; Kaufman, 2003; Schroeder and Bada, 1976; Wehmiller, 2013; Wehmiller, 1977; Wehmiller and Belknap, 1978).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: The Laetoli discovery has fuelled the analysis of ancient proteins from other mineral matrices, namely tooth enamel.

evidence: Supported by citations to subsequent studies on tooth enamel

claim: Ancient proteins from tooth enamel have been used to reconstruct phylogenies.
